prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- If he knew then what he knows now, he might have made some different decisions before the start of the Iraq war in 2003, the outgoing chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff told reporters Friday. Outgoing Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Peter Pace says he now thinks more troops were needed at the war's start. "One of the mistakes I made in my assumptions going in was that the Iraqi people and the Iraqi Army would welcome liberation, that the Iraqi Army, given the opportunity, would stand together for the Iraqi people and be available to them to help serve the new nation," Gen. Peter Pace said. But "they disintegrated in the face of the coalition's first several weeks of combat, so they weren't here," Pace said. Had he known that would happen, he would have recommended more troops be sent at the outset of the Iraq war, he said. In addition, Pace said, if he had been asked in January 2006 whether the United States should build up its Army and Marine Corps contingents in Iraq, he would have said no, because the plan at the time was to build and equip an Iraqi Army and turn over security duties to it. The force was built and equipped, Pace said, but the February bombing of the Golden Mosque -- one of the holiest Shiite sites -- ignited long-simmering tensions between Sunni and Shiite Muslims, further destabilizing the region and cutting short any plans for U.S. troop reduction. Thousands of people have died in reprisal killings and bombings since the attack. Still, Pace said, "Given what I knew at the time, I'm comfortable with the recommendations that I made." Any errors that were made are to be learned from, he added. Watch how Pace details the mistakes made at Iraq war's start » . And he continued to voice his support for the Iraq invasion. "Twenty-six million Iraqis have the opportunity now," he said. "They are working their way through 3½ decades of being trod upon, held down, no opportunity at all for freedom of expression, for living their lives the way they wanted to, for picking [their] leaders." Pace will retire when his two-year term ends this month. Also Friday, Defense Secretary Robert Gates -- in his first public comments since President Bush announced Thursday night he was accepting the Iraq troop level recommendation of Gen. David Petraeus -- noted all Bush's senior military advisers are in agreement with those recommendations. Gates said he asked Pace and Adm. William Fallon, the head of U.S. Central Command, to begin examining U.S. options in Iraq months ago, knowing that Petraeus -- the top U.S. commander in Iraq -- was doing the same. "I wanted the president this month to have the benefit of more than one senior military voice as he considered the next steps in Iraq," Gates said. "I also did not want Gen. Petraeus hanging out there all by himself. "While the analyses of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, CentCom and Gen. Petraeus varied in emphasis and approach, all of the president's senior military advisers are in full agreement with the recommendations made by Gen. Petraeus," he said. The United States' next steps in Iraq, among other things, "had to avoid even the appearance of American failure," Gates said. "Extremist Islam was dramatically empowered by defeating the Soviet Union in Afghanistan. The first attack against us by the extremists, the World Trade Center in 1993, was launched from Afghanistan just four years after the last Soviet soldier left there. "Should the jihadists be able to claim a victory in Iraq over the United States, the sole remaining superpower, I believe it would empower them worldwide far, far more than their victory over the Soviets," Gates said. "The regional consequences would be significant and highly destabilizing." E-mail to a friend .

outputs.L1:
**WASHINGTON (CNN) —** Had he known then what he knows now, he might have made different decisions before the start of the Iraq war in 2003, the outgoing chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff told reporters Friday.

Gen. Peter Pace said he now believes more troops were needed at the outset of the war.

“One of the mistakes I made in my assumptions going in was that the Iraqi people and the Iraqi Army would welcome liberation, that the Iraqi Army, given the opportunity, would stand together for the Iraqi people and be available to them to help serve the new nation,” Pace said.

But “they disintegrated in the face of the coalition’s first several weeks of combat, so they weren’t here,” he said.

Had he known that would happen, Pace said, he would have recommended sending more troops at the outset of the Iraq war.

Pace also said that, had he been asked in January 2006 whether the United States should increase its Army and Marine Corps contingents in Iraq, he would have said no. At the time, the plan was to build and equip an Iraqi Army and transfer security responsibilities to it.

The force was built and equipped, Pace said, but the February bombing of the Golden Mosque—one of the holiest Shiite sites—ignited long-simmering tensions between Sunni and Shiite Muslims, further destabilizing the region and cutting short any plans to reduce U.S. troop levels.

Thousands of people have died in reprisal killings and bombings since the attack.

Still, Pace said, “Given what I knew at the time, I’m comfortable with the recommendations that I made.” Any errors, he added, should serve as lessons.

*Watch Pace detail the mistakes made at the start of the Iraq war »*

Pace also continued to voice his support for the invasion of Iraq.

“Twenty-six million Iraqis have the opportunity now,” he said. “They are working their way through 3½ decades of being trod upon, held down, no opportunity at all for freedom of expression, for living their lives the way they wanted to, for picking [their] leaders.”

Pace will retire when his two-year term ends this month.

Also Friday, Defense Secretary Robert Gates—in his first public comments since President Bush announced Thursday night that he was accepting the Iraq troop-level recommendation of Gen. David Petraeus—noted that all of Bush’s senior military advisers agree with those recommendations.

Gates said he had asked Pace and Adm. William Fallon, head of U.S. Central Command, to begin examining U.S. options in Iraq months earlier, knowing that Petraeus—the top U.S. commander in Iraq—was doing the same.

“I wanted the president this month to have the benefit of more than one senior military voice as he considered the next steps in Iraq,” Gates said. “I also did not want Gen. Petraeus hanging out there all by himself.

“While the analyses of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, CentCom and Gen. Petraeus varied in emphasis and approach, all of the president’s senior military advisers are in full agreement with the recommendations made by Gen. Petraeus,” he said.

The United States’ next steps in Iraq, among other considerations, “had to avoid even the appearance of American failure,” Gates said.

“Extremist Islam was dramatically empowered by defeating the Soviet Union in Afghanistan. The first attack against us by the extremists, the World Trade Center in 1993, was launched from Afghanistan just four years after the last Soviet soldier left there.

“Should the jihadists be able to claim a victory in Iraq over the United States, the sole remaining superpower, I believe it would empower them worldwide far, far more than their victory over the Soviets,” Gates said. “The regional consequences would be significant and highly destabilizing.”

*E-mail to a friend.*
outputs.L2:
WASHINGTON (CNN) — The departing chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff said Friday that, with the benefit of hindsight, he might have chosen a different course before the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

Gen. Peter Pace said he now believes a larger number of troops should have been deployed when the war began.

Pace explained that one of his initial miscalculations was expecting Iraq’s population and military to embrace their liberation. He had assumed the Iraqi Army would remain unified and, once given the chance, help the Iraqi people establish and support a new country.

Instead, the Iraqi military collapsed during the coalition’s first few weeks of fighting and was no longer available to help, he said. Had he anticipated that outcome, Pace added, he would have advised sending additional forces at the beginning of the conflict.

Pace also said that, if he had been asked in January 2006 whether the United States should increase the number of Army and Marine personnel in Iraq, he would have opposed such a move. At that point, the strategy was to create and equip an Iraqi Army and then transfer responsibility for security to it.

Although that force was formed and supplied, Pace said, the February bombing of the Golden Mosque—one of Shiite Islam’s most sacred locations—set off tensions that had long existed between Sunni and Shiite Muslims. The attack further destabilized the area and ended prospects for reducing U.S. troop levels. Thousands have since been killed in retaliatory violence and bombings.

Nevertheless, Pace said he remained satisfied with the advice he had offered based on the information available to him at the time. Any mistakes, he added, should serve as lessons for the future.

He also reaffirmed his support for the decision to invade Iraq. Pace said the country’s 26 million people now have an opportunity after enduring 3½ decades of oppression, during which they lacked freedom of expression, the ability to live as they wished and the right to choose their leaders.

Pace is scheduled to retire when his two-year term concludes later this month.

Also on Friday, Defense Secretary Robert Gates made his first public remarks since President Bush announced Thursday night that he had accepted Gen. David Petraeus’ recommendation on troop levels in Iraq. Gates emphasized that Bush’s senior military advisers unanimously supported Petraeus’ proposals.

Gates said he had instructed Pace and Adm. William Fallon, commander of U.S. Central Command, months earlier to begin evaluating possible U.S. courses of action in Iraq. He knew Petraeus, the senior American commander in the country, was conducting a similar review.

According to Gates, he wanted the president to hear from more than one high-ranking military official while deciding that month what the United States should do next in Iraq. He also did not want Petraeus to be left alone in defending his conclusions.

Although the assessments by the Joint Chiefs of Staff, Central Command and Petraeus differed in their methods and areas of emphasis, Gates said all of the president’s top military advisers fully endorsed Petraeus’ recommendations.

Gates added that any future U.S. strategy in Iraq had to prevent even the impression that America had failed.

He argued that extremist Islam gained substantial strength after the Soviet Union was defeated in Afghanistan. The first extremist assault on the United States—the 1993 World Trade Center attack—originated in Afghanistan only four years after the final Soviet troops withdrew from the country.

If jihadists were able to portray Iraq as a victory over the United States, the world’s only remaining superpower, Gates said, they would be emboldened globally to a far greater degree than they had been by defeating the Soviets. He warned that the effects across the region would be serious and deeply destabilizing.
outputs.L3:
General Peter Pace said that, in retrospect, he would have recommended deploying more U.S. troops at the beginning of the Iraq war if he had known that the Iraqi Army would disintegrate. He acknowledged that his early assessments were based on the mistaken assumption that both the Iraqi people and the country’s military would broadly welcome liberation and help support the creation of a new nation.

Pace said those assumptions continued to shape his advice in January 2006, when he opposed increasing the number of U.S. forces in Iraq. At the time, the strategy centered on building, training, and equipping a new Iraqi Army that could gradually assume responsibility for the country’s security, allowing American troop levels to decline.

That plan was disrupted in February 2006 by the bombing of the Golden Mosque, a major Shiite shrine. The attack intensified sectarian violence between Sunnis and Shiites, further destabilized Iraq, and derailed expectations that U.S. forces could soon be reduced.

Despite the consequences, Pace said he remained comfortable with the recommendations he had made based on the information available to him at the time. He also continued to support the original decision to invade Iraq, even while acknowledging that different assumptions about the Iraqi Army’s collapse would have led him to advocate a larger initial U.S. deployment.
outputs.L4:
Outgoing Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Gen. Peter Pace offered a retrospective assessment of U.S. planning for the 2003 invasion of Iraq, acknowledging that the initial force was too small to provide security after the fall of Saddam Hussein’s government.

Pace said prewar plans had assumed that much of the Iraqi Army would remain intact and could help stabilize the country once major combat operations ended. Instead, Iraqi forces disintegrated, leaving U.S. and coalition troops without the local security structure planners had expected. In hindsight, he concluded, the United States should have deployed more troops at the outset to compensate for the Iraqi Army’s collapse and to maintain order during the transition.

The failure of that central assumption became one of the most consequential errors in the occupation. Coalition forces were required not only to defeat Saddam’s military but also to secure cities, protect infrastructure and confront growing insurgent and sectarian violence. The shortage of reliable Iraqi forces delayed efforts to place responsibility for security in Iraqi hands.

Pace emphasized that the United States later worked to rebuild and train Iraqi military and police units so they could gradually take over security duties. That process became a key element of the broader strategy, with American forces seeking to shift from direct combat operations toward supporting Iraqi-led missions.

Despite his criticism of the original planning, Pace defended the larger purpose of the invasion. He argued that removing Saddam’s regime gave Iraqis an opportunity to build a freer political system and determine their own future. His comments thus combined an acknowledgment of a major military-planning mistake with continued support for the opportunities created by the overthrow of the Iraqi government.
outputs.L5:
**Washington, CNN, and the Iraq War**

WASHINGTON — CNN played a central role in shaping American public understanding of the Iraq War. From its reporting in Washington on political debates and intelligence claims to live coverage from Baghdad, the network provided continuous updates before, during, and after the 2003 invasion.

In Washington, the Bush administration argued that Iraq possessed weapons of mass destruction and represented a threat to international security. CNN reported on these claims, congressional discussions, United Nations inspections, and protests opposing military action. After the invasion, no active stockpiles of such weapons were found, prompting intense scrutiny of the intelligence used to justify the war.

As Iraq entered a prolonged period of instability, coverage shifted toward insurgent violence, sectarian conflict, elections, and the experiences of American troops and Iraqi civilians. The war also sparked a broader debate in Washington about foreign policy, media responsibility, and the human and financial costs of military intervention.

U.S. planners therefore expected Iraqis to take over governing and securing the country much sooner than proved possible, and they did not adequately anticipate the post-invasion disorder and insurgency.

Defense Secretary Robert Gates said Gen. David Petraeus would reassess conditions in March 2008 and could recommend troop reductions beyond the five combat brigades already scheduled to leave by July. Gates said he hoped conditions would permit a faster drawdown—potentially to about 100,000 U.S. troops by the end of 2008—but emphasized that he would not prejudge Petraeus’s recommendations.
